name: End-tidal CO2
summary: End-tidal CO2 refers to the partial pressure or maximal concentration of carbon dioxide exhaled at the end of a breath, serving as a vital monitoring parameter in emergency airway management, confirmation of endotracheal tube placement, and monitoring CPR quality.

name: Orotracheal Intubation
summary: Orotracheal intubation is a standard emergency airway management technique where a breathing tube is passed through the mouth and vocal cords into the trachea to secure ventilation.

name: Rapid sequence intubation
summary: Rapid sequence intubation is an advanced airway management technique involving simultaneous administration of a sedative and a neuromuscular blocking agent to rapidly secure the airway of a patient at high risk of aspiration.

name: Macintosh Blade
summary: A curved laryngoscope blade designed to seat in the vallecula to indirectly elevate the epiglottis and expose the vocal cords during endotracheal intubation.

name: Vallecula
summary: An anatomical depression situated anterior to the epiglottis at the base of the tongue, serving as the key landmark where the tip of a curved laryngoscope blade is engaged during endotracheal intubation.

name: Etomidate
summary: A short-acting IV sedative-hypnotic that enhances GABA-A signaling, used as a hemodynamically stable induction agent for Rapid Sequence Intubation (RSI).
bnf_dosage:
Induction of anaesthesia

[BY SLOW INTRAVENOUS INJECTION]
• Adult: 150–300 micrograms/kg (max. per dose 60 mg), to be administered over 30-60 seconds (60 seconds in patients in whom hypotension might be hazardous)
• Elderly: 150–200 micrograms/kg (max. per dose 60 mg), to be administered over 30-60 seconds (60 seconds in patients in whom hypotension might be hazardous)

name: Preoxygenation
summary: The administration of high-flow supplemental oxygen prior to RSI to replace lung nitrogen with oxygen and significantly prolong safe apnea time.

name: Laryngeal Mask Airway
summary: The laryngeal mask airway (LMA) is a supraglottic airway device designed to maintain a patent airway and facilitate oxygenation and ventilation without entering the trachea. It consists of an airway tube connected to an elliptical cuff that sits in the hypopharynx and forms a low-pressure seal around the laryngeal inlet. In emergency medicine and resuscitation, it serves as a primary rescue device in 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' (CICO) scenarios, a bridge to a definitive airway, or a conduit for endotracheal intubation. Sizing is primarily based on patient weight (e.g., size 3 for 30–50 kg, size 4 for 50–70 kg, size 5 for >70 kg). Second-generation LMAs incorporate a gastric drainage port to allow decompression and reduce aspiration risk, as well as higher seal pressures. While LMAs do not provide definitive protection against gastric aspiration compared to a cuffed endotracheal tube, their insertion is rapid, technically simpler than direct or video laryngoscopy, and does not require visualization of the vocal cords or manipulation of the cervical spine.

name: Propofol
summary: Propofol is a short-acting, intravenously administered hypnotic and sedative agent widely used in emergency medicine, critical care, and anesthesia for rapid sequence intubation (RSI) induction, procedural sedation, and maintenance of mechanical ventilation sedation. Its primary mechanism of action involves potentiation of GABA-A receptor activity, leading to increased chloride conductance, hyperpolarization of neuronal membranes, and generalized central nervous system depression, along with minor NMDA receptor inhibition. It exhibits rapid onset (30–45 seconds) and a brief duration of clinical effect (5–10 minutes following bolus administration) due to rapid lipophilic tissue redistribution and hepatic metabolism. Major clinical adverse effects include dose-dependent systemic hypotension (caused by decreased systemic vascular resistance and negative inotropy), respiratory depression/apnea, and intense burning pain on peripheral intravenous injection (often mitigated by pretreatment with lidocaine). High-dose (>4–5 mg/kg/h) or prolonged (>48 hours) infusions carry the risk of Propofol-Related Infusion Syndrome (PRIS), a life-threatening condition characterized by severe refractory metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis, hyperlipidemia, hepatomegaly, renal failure, and refractory bradyarrhythmias or asystole.

name: Rocuronium
affiliation: Emergency Medicine / Anesthesiology / Nondepolarizing Neuromuscular Blocker
sect_or_affiliation: Emergency Medicine / Anesthesiology / Nondepolarizing Neuromuscular Blocker
summary: Rocuronium is an intermediate-acting aminosteroid nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent (NMBA). It competitively blocks nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate, inhibiting skeletal muscle depolarization and producing flaccid paralysis without fasciculations. In emergency medicine, it is a primary paralytic agent for rapid sequence intubation (RSI). At standard RSI dosing of 1.0 to 1.2 mg/kg IV (ideal/adjusted body weight), it achieves excellent intubating conditions in approximately 45 to 60 seconds, comparable to succinylcholine, with an effective duration of paralysis lasting 40 to 60+ minutes. It is the preferred NMBA when succinylcholine is contraindicated (e.g., hyperkalemia, extensive burns >48–72 hours, crush injury, denervating neuromuscular disease, personal/family history of malignant hyperthermia). It has no analgesic, sedative, or amnestic effects, requiring proactive post-intubation sedation and analgesia to prevent patient awareness. Rocuronium is primarily eliminated by the liver and biliary system, with secondary renal excretion; its action can be rapidly and specifically reversed by the selective cyclodextrin binder sugammadex (16 mg/kg IV for immediate post-RSI rescue reversal; 2–4 mg/kg IV for standard reversal depending on twitch depth) or traditional anticholinesterase/anticholinergic combinations (neostigmine and glycopyrrolate) once spontaneous recovery has initiated.
